strengths: The paper addresses a real and well-motivated bottleneck in salient object detection (data scarcity and annotation ambiguity), and unifies DIS and HR-SOD under a generalization-oriented evaluation protocol, which is a sensible reframing of the field.

The multi-modal label extraction pipeline (FLUX DiT intermediate features + concept attention maps + DINO-v3 features) is a clever way to obtain pixel-precise masks without a teacher-bounded pseudo-labeler, and the ablation in Table 6 convincingly shows all three modalities are complementary.

The released S3OD dataset (139,981 images, >2x all prior SOD datasets combined) is a substantial community resource, and the multi-stage quality filtering plus manual verification on 1,000 samples (Appendix B) and FID/IS comparisons against MaskFactory/DatasetDM support dataset quality.

Empirical results are strong and broad: large cross-dataset generalization gains (MAE reductions of 20.7%-50% on DIS benchmarks when trained on synthetic data alone), new SOTA on DIS-5K, and comparisons to relevant synthetic-data baselines (MaskFactory, DatasetDM) in Table 4.

Multiple ablations (iterative generation rounds, backbone, number of masks, prompt generation) and an efficiency table give the evaluation reasonable depth, and the multi-mask decoder with relaxed multiple-choice learning is a clean, well-motivated mechanism for annotation ambiguity.
weaknesses: Potential confound in headline claims: S3OD uses a DINO-v3 ViT-B backbone while compared baselines (BiRefNet, InSPyReNet, MVANet) use older backbones. Table 7 shows DINO-v3 alone yields a large gain over Swin-B (~3 F-measure points), so it is unclear how much of the SOTA and generalization improvement comes from the data pipeline versus the stronger foundation backbone. A baseline with the same backbone trained on real data is needed to isolate the dataset contribution.

Novelty is largely system-level and incremental: DPT with a modern backbone, multiple-choice learning (Guzman-Rivera et al.), concept attention (Helbling et al.), and diffusion-feature dataset synthesis (DatasetDM) are all existing components; the contribution is their combination and engineering rather than a new method or insight.

The S3OD* oracle metric (best match over three predicted masks against ground truth) is not comparable to other methods and is used to argue for the architecture; this is a self-favorable evaluation choice, and the claim that it 'confirms' ambiguity-aware modeling is useful is not directly supported.

Label quality is validated only by the authors: manual verification of 1,000 self-generated samples and a VLM-based filter. There is no comparison against human annotations on real images, and systematic biases inherited from FLUX/DINO-v3 features (e.g., failure modes on thin structures, similar textures) are not analyzed.

Reproducibility concerns: the pipeline depends on several large/proprietary or weakly-specified components (FLUX-Krea checkpoint, GPT-generated prompts, Gemma-3 filtering, an unexplained 'separate large model trained without FLUX features' for consistency filtering). Key hyperparameters of the iterative reweighting (alpha, beta) are given but their sensitivity is not.

The iterative generation framework shows only modest gains in Table 5 (~3.6% F-measure on DIS) and only 3 rounds are tested; the framing as a major contribution ('iterative generation framework') is stronger than the evidence.

Some writing/claim issues: mixed percentages (error-rate reductions reported inconsistently as MAE reductions), typos ('131% more' vs '2x more'), and Table 2's comparison mixes models trained on different real datasets without fully controlled conditions.

strengths: Addresses a real and important problem: data scarcity and annotation ambiguity in SOD/DIS, with a clear motivation connecting the two subtasks.

Large-scale resource: a 139k-image synthetic dataset with pixel-precise masks, substantially larger than all existing SOD datasets combined, with a reasonably well-documented multi-modal generation pipeline (FLUX DiT features, concept attention maps, DINO-v3 features) and multi-stage filtering.

Comprehensive experimental protocol: cross-dataset generalization (Table 2), standard SOTA comparison (Table 3), comparison against other synthetic data methods (Table 4), and ablations covering iterative generation, feature modalities, backbone, number of mask hypotheses, and prompt generation (Tables 5-8).

Reported gains are substantial in places: cross-dataset MAE reductions of 20-50%, and notable improvements on DIS-5K and DUT-OMRON in the fine-tuned setting; the efficiency table (Table 10) shows a favorable FLOPs/FPS trade-off.
Useful qualitative analyses, including the oracle-style S3OD* evaluation that exposes annotation ambiguity in existing benchmarks, and detailed prompting/filtering methodology in the appendix.
weaknesses: Confounded SOTA comparisons: the fine-tuned model is first pretrained on 139k synthetic images while all baselines (BiRefNet, MVANet, InSPyReNet) are not, and S3OD uses a DINO-v3 ViT-B backbone while baselines use weaker backbones. The ablation itself shows the backbone accounts for a large share of the gain (Table 7: 884 vs 914 F-measure on DIS-5K for Swin-B vs DINO-v3 with 1 mask). There is no control experiment (e.g., BiRefNet or the same DPT architecture with DINO-v3 trained on real data) to isolate the contribution of the synthetic data and the multi-mask decoder from the backbone and pretraining scale.

The multi-modal supervision pipeline is an engineering combination of existing components (diffusion internal features, concept attention following Helbling et al., DINO features, DatasetDM-style decoding) without a clearly articulated novel technical insight; the multi-mask decoder applies well-known multiple-choice learning (Guzman-Rivera et al.) to a standard DPT head.

Oracle-style reporting is problematic: S3OD* computes metrics with the best match over three predicted masks against ground truth, which is not a valid comparison against single-output methods; while the authors acknowledge this, presenting it alongside SOTA tables invites over-interpretation, and no human study demonstrates that multiple hypotheses genuinely reflect annotation ambiguity rather than masking model errors.

The iterative generation framework yields only modest gains (Table 5: ~3.6% F-measure over three rounds), and its hyperparameters (alpha=8, beta=0.5, w_min/w_max) appear hand-tuned without sensitivity analysis; the novelty over standard hard-example mining / curriculum sampling is limited.

Mask quality is validated only by a separate large model and a VLM, plus manual verification of just 1,000 samples (1.4% flagged); systematic bias of synthetic masks (e.g., FLUX attention leaking to background objects, systematic boundary errors) is not quantified against real annotations, which matters given the paper's central claim of pixel-precise supervision.

Table 2 comparisons are not apples-to-apples: baselines are trained on small real subtask datasets while S3OD uses 140k images, so 'superior generalization' conflates data scale, synthetic diversity, and architecture. A baseline trained on a comparable volume of real or pseudo-labeled data is missing.

Reproducibility and release plans are unclear: there is no explicit statement that the dataset, prompts, filtering models (the 'separate large model trained without FLUX features' is underspecified), or code will be released; the filtering model architecture is not described, making the pipeline hard to reproduce.

Writing inconsistencies and unsupported claims: dataset size quoted as both 139,000 and 139,981; '131% more than 11 most common benchmarks combined' contradicts Table 1's '2x more than all existing SOD datasets combined'; the loss formulation in Sec. 3.1/3.2 is redundantly and confusingly specified (two decayed regularizers with different gamma values).

Significance is bounded: SOD/DIS benchmarks are already saturated (as the authors themselves note), limiting the broader impact despite the pipeline being nominally applicable to other dense prediction tasks, which is asserted but not demonstrated.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: SOD/DIS/HR-SOD are data-bounded tasks, and the paper convincingly argues that data scarcity—not architecture—is the fundamental bottleneck, unifying subtasks under 'high-fidelity salient segmentation'.

Strong dataset contribution: S3OD (139,981 high-resolution images with pixel-level masks) is more than 2x larger than all existing SOD datasets combined, with a sensible multi-modal supervision pipeline (FLUX DiT features, concept attention maps, DINO-v3 features) that avoids teacher-model bottlenecks.

Comprehensive evaluation: cross-dataset generalization (Table 2), SOTA comparison after fine-tuning (Table 3, with large error reductions on DIS-5K), comparison against competing synthetic data methods (Table 4), plus ablations on iterative generation, feature modalities, number of mask branches, backbones, and prompting strategy.

The multi-mask decoder with multiple-choice learning and decaying auxiliary branch loss is a clean, well-specified approach to inherent annotation ambiguity, and the 'best-of-3 vs GT' analysis (S3OD*) is an interesting probe of annotation ambiguity.

Good transparency on failure handling: multi-stage quality filtering, manual verification of 1,000 samples (Appendix B), and FID/IS comparison to prior synthetic pipelines; the system prompt and pipeline details support reproducibility.

Impressive practical results: 14.0% error reduction on DIS-5K over prior SOTA, and synthetic-only training achieves large cross-dataset MAE reductions, supporting the central claim that generative data scaling generalizes.
weaknesses: Attribution of gains is partially confounded: the DINO-v3 ViT-B backbone is itself a very strong general-purpose feature extractor, and the ablation isolating the backbone effect (Table 7) is only run on DIS-5K fine-tuning; it is unclear how much of the cross-dataset generalization gain in Table 2 comes from the backbone vs. the synthetic data itself.
The multi-mask decoder builds on well-established ideas (multiple-choice learning, IoU-supervised quality heads), so the architectural novelty is modest; the main novelty lies in the data pipeline.

Heavy reliance on large, partially closed models (FLUX-12B, Gemma-3, GPT for prompts, DINO-v3) weakens reproducibility and makes the pipeline costly for other groups; some compute cost analysis for dataset generation is missing.

The S3OD* oracle metric (best match over three masks against ground truth) is not comparable to other methods and risks overstating the practical benefit of ambiguity modeling; its interpretation deserves more care.

Consistency filtering uses a model trained without FLUX features, but the interplay between filtering and the iterative loop (filtering out 'overly ambiguous' samples while the architecture claims ambiguity is valuable) is somewhat contradictory and under-analyzed.
Some headline numbers (e.g., '20-50% error reduction') mix settings (different training data and evaluation protocols); a more precise decomposition would strengthen the claims.
No evaluation of how well the pipeline transfers beyond SOD (the claim that the framework 'is applicable to other dense prediction tasks' is asserted but untested).

strengths: Large-scale, well-motivated contribution: a 139K-image high-resolution synthetic dataset for SOD/DIS with pixel-wise masks, addressing a genuine data-scarcity bottleneck in salient object detection (up to 10 hours of manual annotation per sample).

Novel and technically interesting label-extraction pipeline: combining FLUX DiT feature maps, concept-attention maps, and DINO-v3 features avoids the known weaknesses of attention-only extraction (DatasetDM), mask-conditioned generation (MaskFactory), and teacher-model pseudo-labeling; the ablation in Table 8 convincingly shows all three modalities are complementary.

Very strong and comprehensive evaluation: cross-dataset/cross-task generalization protocol (a fresh and arguably more meaningful evaluation than saturated single-benchmark comparisons), comparisons against BiRefNet, MVANet, InSPyReNet, SAM-based methods, retraining BiRefNet/MVANet on S3OD for fairness (Table 3), comparison to other synthetic-data methods (Table 5), zero-shot transfer to camouflaged object detection (Table 6), plus extensive ablations (iterative generation, modality mix, backbone, number of masks, multi-mask loss regularization) and supplementary domain-gap analysis (FID/IS, UMAP, precision-recall coverage).

Honest and transparent reporting: the oracle variant S3ODNet* is explicitly flagged as not comparable; benchmark saturation is discussed; limitations and compute cost are documented; LLM usage disclosed; the appendix even includes loss-regularization ablations and the full LLM system prompt, aiding reproducibility.

The multi-mask decoder with best-match selection and exponentially decayed auxiliary loss is a sensible adaptation of multiple-choice learning, and the branch-collapse analysis (Appendix G, Table 15) is a nice addition showing why the decay regularizer is necessary.

Clear practical impact: models trained purely on synthetic data generalize well across DIS, HR-SOD, and even COD benchmarks, and pretraining on S3OD consistently improves fine-tuned state-of-the-art results.
weaknesses: Potential confound in headline comparisons: S3ODNet uses a DINO-v3 backbone while most baselines use older backbones (Swin, ResNet, etc.), so some of the reported generalization gains may come from the stronger foundation backbone rather than the synthetic data itself. Table 3/14 partially mitigates this (retraining BiRefNet/MVANet on S3OD and showing S3ODNet still wins), but an ablation of S3ODNet with the same backbone as key baselines trained on real data would strengthen the claims.

The multi-mask decoder gains are modest: Table 9 shows only ~0.5% Fm improvement from 1 to 3 masks (.909 to .914), and the oracle S3ODNet* gap, while interesting, is evaluated with ground-truth access and cannot be directly benchmarked. The 'ambiguity-aware architecture' contribution feels somewhat oversold relative to its measured benefit, and its core idea (multiple-choice learning / MHP) is well established.

The iterative generation framework (Section 4.2) yields relatively small improvements (Table 7: ~0.1-0.3% Fm across rounds despite tripling data), so its contribution as one of the three headline claims is not strongly supported by the evidence.

Some pipeline details raise questions about potential circularity/bias: consistency filtering uses 'a separate large model trained without FLUX features' — insufficient detail on how this model was trained, and filtering synthetic labels by model self-agreement may systematically remove exactly the ambiguous hard cases the paper argues are valuable; also VLM-based semantic validation thresholds (e.g., >70% coverage, <=5 components) appear heuristic and unvalidated.

Claims of '20-50% error reduction' are based on MAE deltas in cross-dataset settings where the baselines are trained on mismatched single-domain datasets while the proposed method is trained on 139K synthetic images — scale and data diversity, not just method, drive the comparison; the fairer controlled comparisons show smaller but still solid gains.

Category taxonomy limited to ImageNet classes (1,676 unique objects vs. DIS-5K's 758) — the diversity advantage over existing datasets is real but less dramatic than the image-count ratio suggests; no analysis of failure cases on object types outside the taxonomy.

Some writing/presentation issues (e.g., Table 4 in-text error-reduction percentages not clearly traceable to specific numbers, 'Mean Average Error' should be 'Mean Absolute Error', inconsistent notation λmask definition), and no code/dataset release commitment is explicitly stated, which matters given the paper's resource-oriented contribution.

strengths: Ambitious and well-executed data generation pipeline: combining FLUX DiT feature maps, concept attention maps, and DINO-v3 features is a sensible multi-modal supervision design, and the multi-stage quality filtering (consistency, mask quality, semantic validation) is thorough and clearly described.

Comprehensive evaluation across DIS, HR-SOD, low-resolution SOD, and transfer to camouflaged object detection, with a large number of baselines, ablations (feature modalities, iterative rounds, multi-mask decoder, backbone, loss parameters), and supporting analyses (UMAP domain gap, precision/recall coverage, FID/IS).
The cross-dataset generalization evaluation protocol is a valuable reframing for a benchmark-saturated field, and the observation that SOD benchmarks have saturated is well supported by the results.

The multi-mask decoder with best-match (multiple-choice learning) supervision, IoU-score-based test-time selection, and the decaying auxiliary loss is a reasonable, well-motivated design for handling annotation ambiguity, and the branch-collapse analysis in the appendix is insightful.
Generous implementation detail (prompts, system prompt, training cost, efficiency table) improves reproducibility.
weaknesses: Critical confound in the headline claim: the 'synthetic-only' model uses a DINO-v3 ViT-B backbone while the main baselines (BiRefNet, InSpyreNet, MVANet) use older/weaker backbones. Without a DINO-v3-backboned baseline trained on real data, the reported 20-50% error reductions cannot be cleanly attributed to the synthetic data rather than the backbone. Table 3 partially mitigates this (BiRefNet/MVANet retrained on S3OD) but does not close the loop with a strong backbone trained on real data.

Circularity in the 'no real data' claim: the mask-decoding module itself is trained with supervision from DIS-5K, HR-SOD, UHRSOD, and DUTS real annotated datasets (Sec. 4.1). The pipeline therefore depends on real pixel-precise labels; 'models trained only on synthetic data' is an overstatement that should be stated much more carefully.

Possible train-test contamination: the synthetic images are generated by FLUX, which was trained on web-scale data likely containing the evaluation benchmarks. No analysis (e.g., near-duplicate detection against test sets) is provided, and a FID of 1.74 against real data raises suspicion of memorization rather than genuine coverage.

The iterative generation framework, advertised as a core contribution, yields marginal gains (e.g., Fm .879→.881 over three rounds on DIS; most metrics essentially flat), which does not justify the framing or the added complexity.

The ambiguity-aware architecture's practical benefit is unclear: the multi-mask gain over a single mask (Table 9: .909→.914 Fm) is small, and the S3ODNet* variant reporting the best match over three predicted masks against ground truth is an oracle evaluation that cannot be compared to baselines; no non-oracle demonstration of ambiguity handling on real ambiguous data is provided.

Some claims are imprecise or inflated: relative MAE reductions ('50.0%', '24.8%') on near-saturated metrics overstate practical significance; Table 8 shows DINO-v3 features alone recover most of the performance (e.g., .913 vs .917 Fm), weakening the multi-modal fusion narrative; Table 10 contains an apparent typo ('.98.1'), and there are other polish issues (e.g., 'BiReftNet').

No discussion of statistical significance, variance over seeds, or code/dataset release plans; given that the dataset is the central artifact, its public availability materially affects the contribution's impact.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: SOD/DIS/HR-SOD are bottlenecked by expensive pixel-precise annotation and deterministic single-output predictions; the paper targets both data scarcity and label ambiguity with a coherent pipeline.

Substantial and well-executed data contribution: a 139k-image high-resolution synthetic dataset (2x all prior SOD data combined) generated via a multi-modal diffusion pipeline (FLUX DiT features + concept-attention maps + DINO-v3 features), with multi-stage quality filtering (consistency, VLM mask quality, semantic validation) and a quantitative domain-gap analysis (UMAP, precision/recall for images and masks).

Strong empirical results: synthetic-only training yields large cross-dataset generalization gains; fine-tuned models set new SOTA on DIS-5K and DUT-OMRON; convincing zero-shot and fine-tuned transfer to camouflaged object detection; comparisons against BiRefNet, MVANet, InSPyReNet, and SAM-based models (HQ-SAM, DIS-SAM) are extensive.

Good validation of the dataset itself: retraining BiRefNet and MVANet on S3OD (Table 3) shows the gains are not specific to the proposed architecture, and comparisons against alternative synthetic-data methods (MaskFactory, DatasetDM) under matched data budgets (Table 5) directly support the generation-pipeline claims.

Thorough ablations covering modalities (Table 8), backbone (Table 9), multi-mask count, iterative generation rounds (Table 7), and multi-mask loss regularization with diversity metrics (Table 15), plus honest reporting of limitations, the oracle evaluation caveat, and compute costs.
Ablation of modality combinations (Table 8) convincingly demonstrates that diffusion features and DINO-v3 features are complementary, supporting the central multi-modal supervision claim.
weaknesses: Potential confound between dataset and backbone: the proposed model uses DINO-v3 while most baselines use older backbones (Swin, PVT). Table 9 (Swin-B vs DINO-v3, .884 vs .909 Fm) suggests a large share of the improvement may come from the foundation backbone rather than the synthetic data; a fully controlled comparison (baselines with DINO-v3 backbones, or S3ODNet with matched backbones) is missing.

The architectural contribution is modest and gains from it are small: multi-mask prediction is a direct application of multiple-choice learning / MHP (Rupprecht et al., 2017), and Table 9 shows N=3 vs N=1 improves Fm by only ~0.5 points on DIS-5K; the iterative generation ablation (Table 7) also yields only ~1-2 point gains, weaker than the paper's headline narrative suggests.

The multi-mask/ambiguity story is partially undermined by the supervision setup: only a single ground-truth annotation exists per image, so the model is trained toward one interpretation per sample; the claim of 'handling inherent ambiguity' is supported mainly by the oracle evaluation (S3ODNet*), which uses ground truth and is admittedly not comparable to other methods. No human study or analysis of when/why alternative masks correspond to genuinely valid interpretations is provided.

Circularity in the label-extraction pipeline: the mask decoder that converts multi-modal features into supervision is trained on real labeled datasets (DIS-5K, UHRSOD, DUTS, etc.), so the 'eliminating teacher bottlenecks' claim is overstated — the pipeline still depends on real annotated data for the label extractor, and its ceiling is inherited.

Some inconsistencies and presentation issues reduce confidence: the manual quality check reports 1.4% minor issues and 0.1% missing foreground while the abstract-level claims are stronger; Table 10 contains a typo ('.98.1'); the abstract's '20-50% error reduction' aggregates heterogeneous benchmark-specific numbers; the FP-DIS/UHRSD entries in Table 14 show irregular formatting.

Reproducibility is nontrivial: the pipeline depends on multiple large closed/semi-closed models (FLUX-Krea, DINO-v3, Gemma-3, GPT-4 for prompts), and training requires 8xH200-class compute; no code or data release statement is evident in the manuscript, which matters for a dataset-contribution paper.

FID/IS comparisons (Table 11) against MaskFactory/DatasetDM are somewhat unfair since those methods use much older diffusion backbones; the paper partially acknowledges this but still uses the numbers to support superiority of the method rather than the generator.
